note: What kind of thing a file is, declared by extension rather than sniffed. Extension is a claim the filename makes, not a fact about the bytes — so the kind is recorded at basis 'derived' and never at 'confirmed'. A .mov that is really a .mp4 is mislabelled here and the report says nothing to the contrary.

kinds.scanner_cannot_read: duration, sample rate, channels — none of these are in the directory entry. Reading them means opening and parsing each file, which is a different job from scanning and is not done here.
kinds.note: A session file (.logicx, .als, .band) is a bundle, not a track. It is a directory on disk, so the scan walks into it and reports its contents. That inflates the count and it is not an error — the parts are files.

kinds.scanner_cannot_read: duration, resolution, frame rate — same reason as audio.
kinds.note: Video is where the duplicate question pays for itself: one ten-minute export at three bitrates is three files with three hashes and one work. They are iterations, not duplicates, and only a confirmed stem rule can tell them apart.

kinds.scanner_cannot_read: EXIF. Capture date is not modification time and the two disagree constantly — a photo taken in 2019 and copied in 2024 has a 2024 mtime. Ordering an image series by mtime is therefore wrong more often than it is right, and the iterative verdict says mtime, never 'when it was taken'.
page count, word count, embedded title.

fallback.note: Anything unlisted. It is counted and reported, never dropped. A store where 'other' is the largest kind is telling you the kind list is wrong, which is worth knowing.

load_bearing: The scan reads the directory entry and nothing else: name, size, modification time. Every richer property an audio, video or image file has — duration, resolution, capture date — requires opening the file. That is a second pass, not this one, and until it is written the administrator must not imply it knows any of them.
